```{r}
# Every plot of lab data on these slides is the notebook's own chunk (my202-09-lab-student.qmd; the line numbers
# on the slides refer to it). The data sit next to the notebook in W9/notebooksanddata (git-ignored).
library("quanteda")
library("quanteda.textstats")
library("quanteda.textplots")
library("textrecipes")
library("tidyverse")
library("tidymodels")
library("vip")
library("shapviz")
library("ggraph")
library("igraph")
library("patchwork")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "../notebooksanddata")
options(width = 50, tibble.print_min = 4, tibble.print_max = 4, pillar.max_extra_cols = 0)

theme_slide <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
          plot.title = element_text(size = 13.5, face = "bold"), plot.title.position = "plot")
}
red <- "#E2001A"; dark <- "#8C0014"; pink <- "#F28A94"; grey <- "#6B6B6B"; navy <- "#1F4E79"; green <- "#1D7A46"
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
big <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
esc <- function(x) htmltools::htmlEscape(x)
```

```{r}
#| label: data
#| include: false
# ---- Part I, as in the notebook (student lines 46–52, 65–126). The first chunk is empty in the workbook.
nhs_reviews <- read_csv("data/NHS-reviews.csv") |> drop_na(review_positive)
nhs_corpus <- corpus(nhs_reviews, text_field = "review_text")
tok_clean <- tokens(nhs_corpus, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE)
nhs_tokens <- tok_clean |> tokens_remove(pattern = stopwords("en"))
dfm_full <- dfm(nhs_tokens)
nhs_dfm <- dfm_full |> dfm_trim(min_termfreq = 12)
dfm_stop <- dfm(tok_clean)                               # line 144: what if the stopwords stay in?
n_class <- table(nhs_reviews$review_positive)
len <- tibble(ntoken = ntoken(nhs_tokens), positive = docvars(nhs_tokens)$review_positive)
len_med <- tapply(len$ntoken, len$positive, median)
stopifnot(nrow(nhs_reviews) == 1986, nfeat(dfm_full) == 7560, nfeat(nhs_dfm) == 1033, len_med[["Negative"]] > 1.5 * len_med[["Positive"]],
          all(names(topfeatures(dfm_stop, 4)) %in% stopwords("en")), names(topfeatures(nhs_dfm, 1)) == "appointment",
          all(nhs_reviews$review_positive[nhs_reviews$star_rating >= 3] == "Positive"), all(c("not", "at", "all") %in% stopwords("en")))

# ---- Part II, as in the notebook (student lines 170–179, 189–216)
positive_lgl <- docvars(nhs_dfm)$review_positive == "Positive"
tstat <- textstat_keyness(nhs_dfm, target = positive_lgl)
key <- as_tibble(tstat)
kw <- function(w, what) key[[what]][key$feature == w]
side_total <- c(pos = sum(nhs_dfm[positive_lgl, ]), neg = sum(nhs_dfm[!positive_lgl, ]))
# the keyness slides say: both sides hold about the same number of words, so an unrelated word splits half and half
stopifnot(abs(side_total[["pos"]] / sum(side_total) - 0.5) < 0.01, key$feature[1] == "thank", key$feature[nrow(key)] == "told",
          abs(kw("surgery", "chi2")) < 1, kw("thank", "n_target") == 319, kw("thank", "n_reference") == 10)
nhs_bigram_counts <-
  nhs_tokens |>
  tokens_ngrams(n = 2, concatenator = " ") |>
  dfm() |>
  textstat_frequency() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(bigram = feature, n = frequency) |>
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") |>
  slice_max(n, n = 60, with_ties = FALSE)
bg <- function(a, b) nhs_bigram_counts$n[nhs_bigram_counts$word1 == a & nhs_bigram_counts$word2 == b]
stopifnot(nhs_bigram_counts$word1[1] == "get", nhs_bigram_counts$word2[1] == "appointment", length(bg("face", "face")) == 1)

# ---- Part III, as in the notebook (student lines 228–287). The split chunk (239–243) is empty in the workbook.
nhs_model_data <-
  nhs_reviews |>
  select(review_text, positive = review_positive) |>
  mutate(positive = as.factor(positive))
set.seed(123)
nhs_split <- initial_split(nhs_model_data, prop = 0.75, strata = positive)
nhs_train <- training(nhs_split)
nhs_test <- testing(nhs_split)
nhs_rec <-
  recipe(positive ~ review_text, data = nhs_train) |>
  step_tokenize(review_text) |>
  step_stopwords(review_text, language = "en") |>
  step_tokenfilter(review_text, min_times = 10) |>
  step_tfidf(review_text)
model <-
  boost_tree(mtry = 0.03, trees = 2000, learn_rate = 0.01) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  set_engine("xgboost", counts = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
nhs_fit <-
  workflow() |>
  add_recipe(nhs_rec) |>
  add_model(model) |>
  fit(data = nhs_train)

idf <- nhs_fit |> extract_recipe() |> tidy(number = 4) |> select(token, weight)
nhs_matrix <- nhs_fit |> extract_recipe() |> bake(new_data = nhs_train, all_predictors(), composition = "matrix")
n_feat <- ncol(nhs_matrix)
words <- str_remove(colnames(nhs_matrix), "tfidf_review_text_")
doc_n <- setNames(colSums(nhs_matrix > 0), words)
idf_w <- function(w) idf$weight[idf$token == w]
vi_tab <- nhs_fit |> vi() |> mutate(Variable = str_remove(Variable, "tfidf_review_text_"))

# SHAP. The notebook (lines 306–331) hands shapviz() the dense matrix. The model was fitted on a sparse one, in which a word that
# is absent counts as missing, not as 0, so on the dense matrix the booster predicts something else (see the lesson plan).
# Here the booster gets the same sparse input as in training; a check below makes sure the pushes add up to the predictions.
nhs_sparse <- nhs_fit |> extract_recipe() |> bake(new_data = nhs_train, all_predictors(), composition = "dgCMatrix")
shap <- shapviz(extract_fit_engine(nhs_fit), X_pred = xgboost::xgb.DMatrix(nhs_sparse), X = as.data.frame(nhs_matrix))
colnames(shap) <- str_remove(colnames(shap), "tfidf\\_review\\_text\\_")
S <- get_shap_values(shap); base <- get_baseline(shap)
p_neg_train <- predict(nhs_fit, nhs_train, type = "prob")$.pred_Negative
shap_rank <- names(sort(colMeans(abs(S)), decreasing = TRUE))
dense_wrong <- mean((predict(extract_fit_engine(nhs_fit), nhs_matrix) > 0.5) == (nhs_train$positive == "Negative"))
# positive SHAP = towards "Negative" (R's first level); the pushes plus the start give exactly the workflow's prediction
stopifnot(n_feat == 100, max(abs(plogis(rowSums(S) + base) - p_neg_train)) < 1e-4, abs(plogis(base) - mean(nhs_train$positive == "Negative")) < 0.01,
          shap_rank[1] == "thank", setequal(shap_rank[1:5], vi_tab$Variable[1:5]), mean(S[nhs_matrix[, words == "thank"] > 0, "thank"]) < -1,
          mean(S[nhs_matrix[, words == "told"] > 0, "told"]) > 0.5)

aug_test <- augment(nhs_fit, new_data = nhs_test); aug_train <- augment(nhs_fit, new_data = nhs_train)
cm <- conf_mat(aug_test, positive, .pred_class)
f1_scores <-
  bind_rows(
    aug_train |> f_meas(truth = positive, estimate = .pred_class) |> mutate(set = "Training"),
    aug_test |> f_meas(truth = positive, estimate = .pred_class) |> mutate(set = "Testing")
  ) |>
  mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("Training", "Testing")))
f1_of <- function(s) f1_scores$.estimate[f1_scores$set == s]
n_wrong <- sum(aug_test$.pred_class != aug_test$positive)
odd_words <- intersect(c("one", "just", "need", "still", "never"), vi_tab$Variable[1:20])
stopifnot(length(odd_words) >= 2)
f1_pos <- f_meas(aug_test, truth = positive, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
# the last discussion question asks for another model: a lasso logistic regression on the same recipe
set.seed(123)
lasso_fit <- workflow() |> add_recipe(nhs_rec) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet")) |> fit(data = nhs_train)
f1_lasso <- augment(lasso_fit, new_data = nhs_test) |> f_meas(truth = positive, estimate = .pred_class) |> pull(.estimate)
stopifnot(f1_of("Training") > f1_of("Testing") + 0.08, f1_of("Testing") > 0.75, abs(f1_lasso - f1_of("Testing")) < 0.05, levels(nhs_train$positive)[1] == "Negative")
```

```{r}
#| label: visuals
#| include: false
# ---- The café: six made-up reviews. One example for the bag of words, TF-IDF and the exit question.
cafe <- tibble(
  review = c("Great coffee, and the staff are so friendly!", "Friendly staff. The coffee was great.", "I love the cakes and the coffee here.",
             "The coffee was cold and the staff were rude.", "We had to wait 20 minutes for a cold coffee.", "Rude staff, and a long wait. Never again!"),
  happy = rep(c("yes", "no"), each = 3))
cafe_corpus <- corpus(cafe, text_field = "review")
cafe_raw <- as.list(tokens(cafe_corpus))
cafe_tokens <- tokens(cafe_corpus, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE) |> tokens_remove(pattern = stopwords("en"))
cafe_dfm <- dfm(cafe_tokens)
dropped <- function(tok) tolower(tok) %in% stopwords("en") | !str_detect(tok, "[[:alpha:]]")
cafe_counts <- colSums(cafe_dfm)[order(-colSums(cafe_dfm))]
# the slides strike out exactly the tokens quanteda drops, and say: coffee is in five of the six reviews
stopifnot(identical(unname(map(cafe_raw, ~ .x[!dropped(.x)])), unname(as.list(cafe_tokens))), nfeat(cafe_dfm) == 12,
          sum(cafe_dfm[, "coffee"] > 0) == 5, sum(cafe_dfm[, "rude"] > 0) == 2)

tk <- function(x, cls = "") paste0('<span class="tk ', cls, '">', esc(x), "</span>", collapse = "")
lab <- function(h, frag = NULL) paste0('<span class="bw-lab ', h, if (is.null(frag)) "" else paste0(' fragment" data-fragment-index="', frag), '">',
                                       c(yes = "happy", no = "unhappy", q = "?")[h], "</span>")
# a word that gets a box on a later click (the text itself is there from the start)
hl <- function(x, words, cls, idx) str_replace_all(x, regex(paste0("\\b(", paste(words, collapse = "|"), ")\\b"), ignore_case = TRUE),
                                                   paste0('<span class="fragment hlw ', cls, '" data-fragment-index="', idx, '">\\1</span>'))
# Slide 3: the six reviews bare; click 1 shows the labels, click 2 boxes the words that gave it away, click 3 boxes "coffee"
read_panel <- function() {
  rows <- map_chr(1:6, function(i) {
    txt <- esc(cafe$review[i]) |> hl(c("great", "friendly", "love"), "pos", 2) |> hl(c("cold", "rude", "wait"), "neg", 2) |> hl("coffee", "neu", 3)
    paste0('<div class="bw-row">', lab(cafe$happy[i], frag = 1), '<div class="bw-body">', txt, "</div></div>")
  })
  paste0('<div class="bw"><p class="bw-title">Six reviews of a café (made up)</p>', paste(rows, collapse = ""), "</div>")
}
dfm_table <- function(extra = NULL, extra_lab = NULL) {
  m <- as.matrix(cafe_dfm)[, names(cafe_counts)]
  cells <- function(v, cls = if_else(v == 0, "z", "nz")) paste0('<td class="', cls, '">', v, "</td>", collapse = "")
  head_row <- paste0("<tr><th></th>", paste0("<th>", colnames(m), "</th>", collapse = ""), "</tr>")
  rows <- map_chr(1:6, ~ paste0("<tr><td>", lab(cafe$happy[.x]), "</td>", cells(m[.x, ]), "</tr>"))
  if (!is.null(extra)) rows <- c(rows, paste0('<tr class="new"><td>', lab(extra_lab), "</td>", if (is.character(extra)) cells(extra, "q") else cells(extra), "</tr>"))
  paste0('<table class="bw-dfm">', head_row, paste(rows, collapse = ""), "</table>")
}
# Slide 6: a seventh review. First the sentence and an empty row, then what the cleaning leaves and the row it gets.
seventh <- "Not friendly at all."
sev_raw <- as.list(tokens(seventh))[[1]]
sev_row <- as.numeric(dfm_match(dfm(tokens(seventh, remove_punct = TRUE) |> tokens_remove(pattern = stopwords("en"))), names(cafe_counts)))
stopifnot(sum(sev_row) == 1, sev_row[names(cafe_counts) == "friendly"] == 1, sum(!dropped(sev_raw)) == 1)
seventh_panel <- function(s) {
  line <- if (s == 1) paste0("“", esc(seventh), "”") else paste(map_chr(sev_raw, ~ tk(.x, if (dropped(.x)) "drop" else "keep")), collapse = "")
  paste0('<div class="bw"><p class="bw-title">', c("A seventh review arrives", "What is left of it: one word")[s], "</p>",
         '<div class="bw-row" style="border-bottom:none">', lab(if (s == 1) "q" else "no"), '<div class="bw-body">', line, "</div></div>",
         dfm_table(if (s == 1) rep("?", length(sev_row)) else sev_row, if (s == 1) "q" else "no"), "</div>")
}
bag_panel <- function(s) {
  title <- c("1 · A corpus: six documents, each with what we know about it",
             "2 · Tokens: cut every review into pieces",
             "3 · Clean: drop punctuation, numbers and stopwords",
             "4 · Count: one row per review, one column per word")[s]
  if (s == 4) {
    body <- dfm_table()
  } else {
    body <- paste(map_chr(1:6, function(i) {
      inner <- switch(s, esc(cafe$review[i]), tk(cafe_raw[[i]]),
                      paste(map_chr(cafe_raw[[i]], ~ tk(.x, if (dropped(.x)) "drop" else "keep")), collapse = ""))
      paste0('<div class="bw-row">', lab(cafe$happy[i]), '<div class="bw-body">', inner, "</div></div>")
    }), collapse = "")
  }
  paste0('<div class="bw"><p class="bw-title">', title, "</p>", body, "</div>")
}

# ---- TF-IDF by hand on café review 4, with textrecipes' own numbers
cafe_rec <- recipe(happy ~ review, data = cafe) |> step_tokenize(review) |> step_stopwords(review) |> step_tfidf(review) |> prep()
cafe_idf <- tidy(cafe_rec, number = 3)
cafe_tfidf <- bake(cafe_rec, NULL) |> rename_with(~ str_remove(.x, "tfidf_review_"))
r4 <- tibble(word = c("coffee", "staff", "cold", "rude")) |>
  mutate(in_reviews = map_int(word, ~ sum(cafe_dfm[, .x] > 0)), tf = 1 / 4,
         idf = cafe_idf$weight[match(word, cafe_idf$token)], tfidf = map_dbl(word, ~ cafe_tfidf[[.x]][4]),
         word = factor(word, levels = rev(word)))
# the slide's two formulas must be the ones textrecipes uses
stopifnot(abs(r4$idf - log(1 + 6 / r4$in_reviews)) < 1e-8, abs(r4$tfidf - r4$tf * r4$idf) < 1e-8, r4$tfidf[3] > 1.5 * r4$tfidf[1])
tfidf_step <- function(s) {
  d <- r4 |> mutate(value = list(tf, idf, tfidf)[[s]],
                    label = list(rep("1 of 4 words = 0.25", 4), paste0("in ", in_reviews, " of 6: ", f2(idf)), paste0("0.25 × ", f2(idf), " = ", f2(tfidf)))[[s]])
  ggplot(d, aes(value, word)) +
    geom_col(fill = c(grey, navy, red)[s], width = 0.62) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.06, size = 5.2, fontface = "bold", colour = "#1A1A1A") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, c(0.6, 3.6, 0.9)[s]), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    theme_slide() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold", colour = "#1A1A1A")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = c("1 · TF: how much of this review is the word?",
                                       "2 · IDF: how rare is the word across reviews?",
                                       "3 · TF × IDF: the number the model gets")[s])
}

# ---- Keyness by hand, on the lab data: where are a word's uses, against an even split?
key_words <- c("thank", "friendly", "helpful", "staff", "surgery", "gp", "appointment", "phone", "told")
key_d <- key |> filter(feature %in% key_words) |> mutate(total = n_target + n_reference, share = n_target / total) |>
  arrange(share) |> mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = feature))
stopifnot(nrow(key_d) == length(key_words))
key_step <- function(s) {
  if (s == 4) {
    return(ggplot(key_d, aes(chi2, feature, fill = chi2 > 0)) +
      geom_col(width = 0.68, show.legend = FALSE) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.5) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = navy, `FALSE` = red)) +
      theme_slide() + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, colour = "#1A1A1A")) +
      labs(x = "Keyness (chi-squared, with a sign)", y = NULL, title = "4 · Keyness: how surprising is the split, and which way?"))
  }
  d <- if (s <= 2) filter(key_d, feature == "thank") else key_d
  long <- d |> transmute(feature, Positive = if (s == 1) 0.5 else share, Negative = 1 - Positive) |>
    pivot_longer(-feature, names_to = "side", values_to = "share") |> mutate(side = factor(side, levels = c("Negative", "Positive")))
  p <- ggplot(long, aes(share, feature, fill = side)) +
    geom_col(width = if (s <= 2) 0.34 else 0.68, alpha = if (s == 1) 0.45 else 1) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Positive = navy, Negative = red), breaks = c("Positive", "Negative"), name = "Uses in reviews that are") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    theme_slide() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, colour = "#1A1A1A"), plot.margin = margin(5, 18, 5, 5)) +
    labs(x = "Share of the word's uses", y = NULL,
         title = c(paste0("1 · If “thank” had nothing to do with mood: ", round(kw("thank", "n_target") + kw("thank", "n_reference")), " uses, half and half"),
                   paste0("2 · In fact: ", round(kw("thank", "n_target")), " in positive reviews, ", round(kw("thank", "n_reference")), " in negative"),
                   "3 · The same count for other words")[s])
  if (s <= 2) p <- p + annotate("label", x = 0.5, y = 1.36, label = "an even split", size = 4.6, fontface = "bold", vjust = 0, label.size = 0)
  p
}

# ---- SHAP for one real training review: a start, a push per word, a prediction
ex <- which(str_detect(nhs_train$review_text, "^Friendly, approachable, they listen"))
stopifnot(length(ex) == 1)
ex_present <- words[nhs_matrix[ex, ] > 0]
ex_push <- S[ex, ex_present][order(-abs(S[ex, ex_present]))]
ex_rest <- sum(S[ex, setdiff(colnames(S), ex_present)])
ex_end <- base + sum(S[ex, ])
# the slide names the four words of this review the model can see, and says the review is positive and predicted positive
stopifnot(setequal(ex_present, c("friendly", "get", "really", "appointment")), names(ex_push)[1:2] == c("friendly", "get"), ex_push[["friendly"]] < -1,
          ex_push[["get"]] > 0.8, nhs_train$positive[ex] == "Positive", plogis(ex_end) < 0.3, abs(plogis(ex_end) - p_neg_train[ex]) < 1e-4)
wf <- tibble(step = c("friendly", "get", "really", "appointment", paste0("the ", n_feat - 4, " absent words")),
             push = c(ex_push[c("friendly", "get", "really", "appointment")], ex_rest)) |>
  mutate(from = base + lag(cumsum(push), default = 0), to = base + cumsum(push), row = row_number())
shap_step <- function(s) {
  show <- c(0, 1, 2, 5, 5)[s]
  d <- wf |> filter(row <= show)
  rows <- c("start", wf$step, "prediction")
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = base, colour = grey, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
    annotate("point", x = base, y = "start", size = 5.5, colour = "#3A3A3A") +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(rows)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = qlogis(c(0.04, 0.72)), breaks = qlogis(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.38, 0.6)), labels = c("5%", "10%", "20%", "38%", "60%")) +
    theme_slide() + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 14, colour = "#1A1A1A")) +
    labs(x = "Chance that the review is negative", y = NULL,
         title = c(paste0("1 · Start: ", pct(plogis(base)), " of the training reviews are negative"),
                   "2 · “friendly” is in the review: a push towards positive",
                   "3 · “get” is in it too: a push back towards negative",
                   "4 · The other words, present and absent, push a little",
                   paste0("5 · Add it all up: ", pct(plogis(ex_end)), " negative, so the model says positive"))[s])
  if (show > 0) p <- p +
    geom_segment(data = d, aes(x = from, xend = to, y = step, yend = step, colour = push > 0), linewidth = 4.2,
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "in"), type = "closed"), linejoin = "mitre", show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(data = d, aes(x = pmax(from, to) + 0.2, y = step, label = formatC(push, format = "f", digits = 2, flag = "+")), hjust = 0, size = 4.4, fontface = "bold") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = red, `FALSE` = navy))
  if (s == 5) p <- p + annotate("point", x = ex_end, y = "prediction", size = 6.5, shape = 23, fill = "white", colour = "black", stroke = 1.8) +
    annotate("label", x = ex_end + 0.14, y = "prediction", label = pct(plogis(ex_end)), hjust = 0, size = 4.6, label.size = 0, fontface = "bold")
  p
}

# ---- The notebook's plots (same code as the student workbook, larger text for the room)
stars_plot <- function(coloured = TRUE) {
  nhs_reviews |> count(star_rating, review_positive) |>
    ggplot(aes(factor(star_rating), n, fill = review_positive)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.7) + geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, size = 4.6) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = if (coloured) c(Positive = navy, Negative = red) else c(Positive = "#9A9A9A", Negative = "#9A9A9A"),
                      name = "review_positive", guide = if (coloured) "legend" else guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 0), theme = theme(legend.text = element_text(colour = "white"), legend.title = element_text(colour = "white")))) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.22))) +
    theme_slide() + theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) + labs(x = "star_rating", y = "Reviews")
}
top_plot <- function() {
  tibble(word = names(topfeatures(nhs_dfm, 12)), n = topfeatures(nhs_dfm, 12)) |>
    ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(word, n))) + geom_col(fill = navy, width = 0.7) +
    theme_slide() + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) + labs(x = "Uses in all reviews", y = NULL, title = "The 12 most used words in the DFM")
}
length_plot <- function() {
  len |>
    ggplot(aes(ntoken, fill = positive)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Positive = navy, Negative = red)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom") +
    labs(x = "Tokens in the review (stopwords removed)", y = "Density", fill = NULL)
}
bigram_plot <- function() {
  set.seed(5)
  nhs_bigram_counts |>
    graph_from_data_frame() |>
    ggraph(layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n, edge_width = n), colour = "grey40",
                   arrow = grid::arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(2, "mm")), end_cap = circle(2, "mm"), show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_node_point(colour = "#00468B", size = 3) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3.9) +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2)) +
    theme_void()
}
vip_plot <- function() {
  vi_tab |>
    slice_max(Importance, n = 20) |>
    mutate(Variable = fct_reorder(Variable, Importance)) |>
    ggplot(aes(Importance, Variable)) +
    geom_col(fill = navy) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) +
    labs(y = NULL)
}
shap_plot <- function(n = 15) {
  sv_importance(shap, kind = "both", show_numbers = TRUE, max_display = n) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) +
    labs(x = "SHAP value")
}
f1_plot <- function() {
  f1_scores |>
    ggplot(aes(set, .estimate, fill = set)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(.estimate, 2)), vjust = -0.5, size = 5) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
    ggsci::scale_fill_lancet() +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "F1-score")
}
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Now it is a table]{.ct}
`r nrow(cafe)` rows, `r nfeat(cafe_dfm)` columns, mostly zeros. *Rude* and *rude* share a column.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 5 minutes. The picture to remember from Part I. Each click is one function in the notebook.

- A corpus is a collection of documents: here six reviews. Each document can carry extra columns: here whether the customer was happy. quanteda calls those document variables, `docvars`.
- Click: cut each review into tokens. A token is a word, a number or a punctuation mark. "20" is a token; so is the full stop.
- Click: throw away what carries no meaning for our question. Punctuation and numbers go. So do the stopwords: a fixed list of `r length(stopwords("en"))` very common English words. What is left (dark boxes) is short: "coffee cold staff rude".
- Click: count. One row per review, one column per word that survived, the count in the cell. Read review 4 across: coffee 1, staff 1, cold 1, rude 1, everything else 0.
- The columns are called features, as in every lab since Lab 3: hence "document-feature matrix".
- Look down the columns: "great" and "friendly" only have counts in happy rows; "cold", "rude" and "wait" only in unhappy rows; "coffee" in nearly all. A model can work with that.
:::

## Corpus, then tokens

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Text as data</span><span class="on">I · Text to table</span><span>II · Which words?</span><span>III · Predict, explain</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 65–113 <span>"Introducing quanteda": given, ready to run</span><i>run together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.5em">nhs_corpus &lt;- <span class="tok">corpus(nhs_reviews,</span> <span class="tok">text_field = "review_text"</span>)

nhs_tokens &lt;-
  <span class="tok">tokens(nhs_corpus,</span>
    <span class="tok">remove_punct = TRUE</span>,
    <span class="tok">remove_symbols = TRUE</span>,
    <span class="tok">remove_numbers = TRUE</span>) |&gt;
  <span class="tok">tokens_remove(</span><span class="tok">pattern = stopwords("en")</span>)</p>
```

1. **Make a corpus.**
2. **The text column.**
3. **Cut into tokens.**
4. **Drop** `.` `,` `!` `?`
5. **Drop** `&` `£` `+` and emoji.
6. **Drop** `20`, `111`, `2021`.
7. **Then take out** …
8. … **the `r length(stopwords("en"))` stopwords.**
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
[Review 3, cut into tokens]{style="display:block;font-size:0.55em;font-weight:700;margin-bottom:4px"}

::: {.r-stack}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
r3 <- as.list(tokens(nhs_corpus[3]))[[1]]
stopifnot(identical(r3[!dropped(r3)], as.list(nhs_tokens[3])[[1]]))
box <- 'style="font-size:0.5em;line-height:1.5;background:#fff;text-align:left;width:100%;min-height:118px"'
cat("<div", box, ">", paste(map_chr(r3, ~ tk(.x, "keep")), collapse = ""), "</div>")
cat('<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"', box, ">", paste(map_chr(r3, ~ tk(.x, if (dropped(.x)) "drop" else "keep")), collapse = ""), "</div>")
```
:::

::: {.ask style="font-size:0.72em"}
Which of these tokens will survive?
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact .dark style="margin-top:0.5em"}
[`r big(sum(ntoken(tokens(nhs_corpus))))` tokens → `r big(sum(ntoken(nhs_tokens)))`]{.ct}
More than half of everything written is punctuation or a stopword.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes. Run lines 71–76, 80–86 and 96–109 together. Nothing to type.

- `corpus()` is step 1 of the café slide. Printing `nhs_corpus` shows the first few reviews. The other five columns travel with the texts: lines 80–86 print them with `docvars()`. We use them again for the colours in the exercise and for the keyness plot.
- `tokens()` is steps 2 and 3. The three `remove_` arguments do the cleaning while cutting. `tokens_remove()` then takes out every token on a list; `stopwords("en")` is that list. Type `stopwords("en")` in the console to see it.
- On the right: the third review, cut into tokens by a bare `tokens()`. Ask which tokens the rest of the chunk will remove. Click: struck out is what goes, and what the model keeps is "always extremely good experience surgery GP's Practice Manager Nurses Receptionists helpful professional". Still readable.
- The teaching moment at line 92: n-grams (pairs of words) come back in Part II; stemming (treating "appointment" and "appointments" as one word) is not used today, which is why both appear in the plots.
:::

## The document-feature matrix

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Text as data</span><span class="on">I · Text to table</span><span>II · Which words?</span><span>III · Predict, explain</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 115–142 <span>the DFM, and the whole pipeline in one chunk</span><i>run together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.anatomy .one}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.6em">nhs_dfm &lt;-
  nhs_tokens |&gt;
  <span class="tok">dfm()</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">dfm_trim(</span><span class="tok">min_termfreq = 12</span>)</p>
```

1. **Count**: one row per review, one column per word, lower case.
2. **Trim** the columns.
3. **Keep a word only if** it is used at least 12 times in all reviews together.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm" style="margin-top:0.5em">
  <div><span class="cl">After dfm()</span><span class="cx">`r big(nrow(nhs_reviews))` rows × `r big(nfeat(dfm_full))` columns</span></div>
  <div><span class="cl">Used once</span><span class="cx">`r big(sum(colSums(dfm_full) == 1))` of the words <small>plesant, explination …</small></span></div>
  <div class="hl"><span class="cl">After trim</span><span class="cx">`r big(nrow(nhs_reviews))` rows × `r big(nfeat(nhs_dfm))` columns</span></div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 3.3
top_plot()
```

::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Why trim?]{.ct}
A word used once cannot tell us anything about **other** reviews. And `r pct(sparsity(nhs_dfm))` of the cells are still 0.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes. Run lines 117–126.

- `dfm()` is step 4 of the café slide: the count table. It also turns everything into lower case.
- Without trimming there are `r big(nfeat(dfm_full))` columns for `r big(nrow(nhs_reviews))` rows: more columns than rows, and half of the words appear exactly once, many of them typos. A column with a single 1 in it is useless for prediction: it only identifies one review.
- `dfm_trim(min_termfreq = 12)` keeps the `r big(nfeat(nhs_dfm))` words used at least 12 times. The text under the chunk talks about a threshold of 10, which gives `r big(nfeat(dfm_trim(dfm_full, min_termfreq = 10)))`; the chunk says 12. Anything near there is fine.
- The chunk at lines 130–140 is the same four steps in one pipe (`eval=FALSE`: it is there to read, not to run).
- The plot: the most used words. Appointments, the surgery, getting something, the phone. Ask what kind of reviews these will be. The word cloud in the exercise shows the same counts.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div><span class="cl">Expected</span><span class="cx">an even split <small>both sides hold about `r big(side_total[["pos"]] / 1000)`,000 words</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="cl">Observed</span><span class="cx">where the uses really are</span></div>

</div>
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Three kinds of word]{.ct}
*thank*, *friendly*: nearly all in positive reviews. *told*: mostly in negative ones. *surgery*, *gp*: half and half.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[One number per word]{.ct}
A chi-squared test of the split. **Large** = far from even. The **sign** says which side: above 0 is typical of positive reviews.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes. The word cloud said how often. Keyness says where.

- The word "thank" is used `r round(kw("thank", "n_target") + kw("thank", "n_reference"))` times. If thanking had nothing to do with whether a review is positive, where would those uses be? Positive reviews are more numerous but shorter, and it happens to even out: both kinds of review contain about `r big(side_total[["pos"]] / 1000)`,000 words in total. So we would expect about half of the uses on each side.
- Click: in fact `r round(kw("thank", "n_target"))` are in positive reviews and `r round(kw("thank", "n_reference"))` in negative ones.
- Click: the same count for eight more words, sorted. Three kinds: words that sit almost entirely in positive reviews, words that sit mostly in negative ones, and words such as "surgery" and "gp" that split evenly. The even ones are this data set's "coffee".
- Click: keyness turns the gap into one number per word. It is the chi-squared test from MY451 or any first statistics course, applied to a two-by-two table: this word or any other word, positive or negative review. quanteda adds a sign so that the direction is visible.
- "appointment" is the most frequent word, and leans negative, but less than "told": a word can be frequent without being telling.
:::

- The notebook's plot shows the 20 words with the highest and the 20 with the lowest keyness. The slide shows 10 of each so that the labels can be read.
- Click: positive reviews are about people and manner: thank, helpful, friendly, caring, professional. "jab" is in there too: the reviews are from 2021, and vaccination clinics were well organised.
- Click: negative reviews are about access: told, get, call, phone, appointment, book, trying, hold, impossible. Hardly a word about the medical care itself. "rude" is the one word on this side about manner.
- That is a finding you could report to a practice manager without any model: the complaints are about the telephone line.


```{r}

tfidf_step(3)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.ask style="font-size:0.75em"}
Four words, each used once. Which say most about **this** review?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm" style="margin-top:0.4em">
  <div><span class="cl">TF</span><span class="cx">count ÷ words in the review <small>term frequency</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="cl">IDF</span><span class="cx">log(1 + reviews ÷ reviews with the word) <small>inverse document frequency</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="cl">TF-IDF</span><span class="cx">TF × IDF</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Common everywhere = worth less]{.ct}
*coffee* is in 5 of 6 reviews, *rude* in 2. Same count, but *rude* gets the larger number.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[IDF looks at all the reviews]{.ct}
So it must be learned from the **training** reviews only: it goes **inside the recipe**, after the split.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes. Back to the café for one slide.

- In the count table this review has four 1s. But "coffee" told us nothing on the first slide, and "rude" told us everything. TF-IDF builds that into the numbers.
- TF, term frequency: what share of the review is this word? Four words survive cleaning, each is one of four: 0.25. In a long review a single mention counts for less.
- Click: IDF, inverse document frequency: how rare is the word across all reviews? "coffee" is in 5 of 6 reviews, "rude" in 2 of 6. The rarer, the larger. The log keeps very rare words from dominating. This is the formula `step_tfidf()` uses.
- Click: multiply. "cold" and "rude" end up with `r f2(r4$tfidf[3])`, "coffee" with `r f2(r4$tfidf[1])`.
- On the lab data: "appointment" is in `r doc_n[["appointment"]]` of `r big(nrow(nhs_train))` training reviews and gets a weight of `r f2(idf_w("appointment"))`; "thank" is in `r doc_n[["thank"]]` and gets `r f2(idf_w("thank"))`.
- Click: the paragraph at line 226. IDF counts reviews. If it counted the test reviews too, the test set would shape the features the model is trained on: the same leak as normalising before splitting in Lab 5. Inside the recipe, the vocabulary and the weights come from the training reviews and are then applied to the test reviews.
:::

## Split first, then the recipe

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Text as data</span><span class="done">I · Text to table</span><span class="done">II · Which words?</span><span class="on">III · Predict, explain</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 226–256 <span>the split chunk (239–243) is empty: type it · the recipe is given</span><i>code together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.anatomy .one}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.5em">nhs_rec &lt;-
  <span class="tok">recipe(positive ~ review_text, data = nhs_train)</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_tokenize(review_text)</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_stopwords(review_text, language = "en")</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_tokenfilter(review_text, min_times = 10)</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_tfidf(review_text)</span></p>
```

1. **Outcome ~ predictor**: one predictor, the raw text.
2. **Cut into tokens**: `tokens()` in Part I.
3. **Drop stopwords**: `tokens_remove()`.
4. **Keep frequent words**: `dfm_trim()`.
5. **Count and weight**: `dfm()`, then TF-IDF.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```r
set.seed(123)
nhs_split <- initial_split(nhs_model_data,
               prop = 0.75, strata = positive)
nhs_train <- training(nhs_split)  # 1,489 reviews
nhs_test  <- testing(nhs_split)   #   497 reviews
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[How many columns come out?]{.ct}
**`r n_feat`**, not 1,000. `step_tokenfilter()` also has `max_tokens`, default 100: only the 100 most used words stay.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 5 minutes. Run lines 228–235, type the split together, run the recipe.

- Lines 228–235 make a two-column table: the text and the label, as a factor. Classification in tidymodels needs a factor outcome (Lab 4).
- The split is Lab 4 and 5: `initial_split()`, 75% for training, `strata = positive` keeps the share of positive reviews the same in both parts. The seed makes everyone's split the same; the workbook does not set one, so type it.
- The recipe: `textrecipes` adds text steps to `recipes`. Each step names the column it works on. Read the four steps against Part I: they are the café slide again.
- Why do it twice? Part I was for looking at the data. The recipe is for modelling: it guarantees that the test reviews play no part in choosing the vocabulary or the IDF weights.
- Click: check with `nhs_rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> ncol()`: `r n_feat + 1`, the outcome plus `r n_feat` words. The notebook's text says "about 1,000 features". `min_times = 10` would allow about that many, but `max_tokens = 100` cuts the list to the 100 most frequent first. The model still works well with 100 words; it is worth knowing what it sees.
:::

## The model: boosted trees, again

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Text as data</span><span class="done">I · Text to table</span><span class="done">II · Which words?</span><span class="on">III · Predict, explain</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 258–287 <span>the model and the workflow: given, ready to run</span><i>run together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.5em">model &lt;-
  <span class="tok">boost_tree(</span><span class="tok">mtry = 0.03</span>, <span class="tok">trees = 2000</span>,
             <span class="tok">learn_rate = 0.01</span>) %&gt;%
  <span class="tok">set_mode("classification")</span> %&gt;%
  <span class="tok">set_engine("xgboost", counts = FALSE)</span>

nhs_fit &lt;- workflow() %&gt;% add_recipe(nhs_rec) %&gt;%
  add_model(model) %&gt;% fit(data = nhs_train)</p>
```

1. **Boosted trees**: Lab 5's relay.
2. **Words offered** per split.
3. **2,000 small trees** in a row.
4. **Each adds 1%** of its fix.
5. **Yes or no** outcome.
6. **xgboost**; `mtry` is a share.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[One tree asks about words]{.ct}
"Is *thank* in the review? If not: is *told*?" Each answer leads to another question, then to a guess.
:::

::: {.card .compact .line}
[Boosting]{.ct}
Every new tree works on the reviews the trees so far get wrong. Small steps (`learn_rate`), so many trees.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[`mtry = 0.03`]{.ct}
3% of `r n_feat` words: each split may choose among **3** random words.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 3 minutes. Run lines 264–275 and 279–287. The fit takes a second or two.

- Nothing here is new: `boost_tree()`, `set_mode()`, `set_engine()`, `workflow()`, `fit()` are Lab 5, with the same `%>%` pipe that chunk used. The only change is what the columns are: TF-IDF numbers for words.
- A tree on text asks whether a word is in the review, or more exactly whether its TF-IDF is above some value. Boosting is the relay from Lab 5: 2,000 small trees, each correcting what is left over.
- `learn_rate = 0.01` and `trees = 2000` go together: tiny steps need many of them.
- `counts = FALSE` makes `mtry` a proportion. Click: the notebook reasons "the square root of 1,000 features, as a share, is about 0.03". With the `r n_feat` words the recipe really produces, 0.03 means 3 words on offer at each split. That is a strong restriction, and one reason the importance is spread over many words later.
- No seed in the workbook before `fit()`, and the choice of words at each split is random: numbers on screens will differ slightly from the slides and from each other.
:::

```{=html}
<p class="quote">"<span class="fragment hlw pos" data-fragment-index="1">Friendly</span>, approachable, they listen instead of assuming, the only down side, it is <span class="fragment hlw pos" data-fragment-index="3">really</span> hard to <span class="fragment hlw neg" data-fragment-index="2">get</span> an <span class="fragment hlw neg" data-fragment-index="3">appointment</span>"</p>
```

::: {.ask style="font-size:0.72em"}
Positive or negative? Which words pull which way?
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[A SHAP value is one push]{.ct}
How far did **this word** move the prediction for **this review**? Left: towards positive. Right: towards negative.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Start + pushes = prediction]{.ct}
Exactly. SHAP explains the model one review at a time.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes. A real review from the training data. Read it aloud and ask the question before the first click: the room will say "friendly" pulls one way and "hard to get an appointment" the other. Each click then boxes the word whose push appears (blue: towards positive, red: towards negative); the four boxed words are the only ones among the model's `r n_feat`.

- A fitted model of 2,000 trees cannot be read like a regression table. SHAP (Shapley values) asks a simpler question for one review at a time: starting from what the model would say about any review, how does each word move the prediction?
- The start: `r pct(plogis(base))` of the training reviews are negative. Before reading anything, that is the model's guess.
- Click: "friendly" is in the review. The model has learned that reviews with "friendly" are rarely negative: a strong push to the left, `r f2(ex_push[["friendly"]])`.
- Click: "get" is there too: "hard to get an appointment". A push back to the right, `r f2(ex_push[["get"]])`.
- Click: "really" and "appointment" push a little. So do the `r n_feat - 4` words that are not in the review: no "told", no "still", no "phone" is mild evidence that this is not a complaint. Together `r f2(ex_rest)`.
- Click: add everything to the start and you get the model's prediction for this review: `r pct(plogis(ex_end))` chance of negative, so it predicts positive. It is right: the patient gave a positive rating, with one reservation, and the pushes show both.
- The numbers on the arrows are on the model's internal scale (log-odds, as in logistic regression, Lab 4). The axis is labelled in percentages so that it can be read; that is why equal pushes look longer in the middle than at the edge.
- Direction: R sorts factor levels alphabetically, "Negative" comes first, and xgboost models the first level. So everything in this part is "towards negative". It comes back in the F1-score.
:::

## Class discussion: read one SHAP value

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Text as data</span><span class="done">I · Text to table</span><span class="done">II · Which words?</span><span class="on">III · Predict, explain</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 304–335 <span>the SHAP chunk and its note</span><i>30 seconds with your neighbour</i></p>
```

::: {.ask}
In one review, the word "thank" has a SHAP value of −2.3. What does that mean?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="opt"><b>A</b>The word "thank" appears 2.3 times less often in this review than on average</div>
  <div class="opt right"><b>B</b>Having "thank" in this review moved the model's prediction a long way towards "positive"</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>C</b>"thank" is an unimportant word, because its value is below zero</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>D</b>Reviews that contain "thank" are 2.3% less likely to be negative</div>
  <div class="fragment why"><b>B.</b> A SHAP value is a push on one prediction. The sign is the direction (below 0: away from "Negative"), the size is the strength. −2.3 is a large push: larger than "friendly" in the last example. Far from 0 in <b>either</b> direction means important.</div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Timing: 1½ minutes. First item to skip if behind.

- Thirty seconds in pairs, a show of hands, click.
- C is the one to argue against: importance is distance from zero, not height. The bar chart in the notebook's SHAP plot is the average **absolute** SHAP value for exactly this reason.
- D mixes up scales: the pushes are not percentage points. The percentages only appear after all pushes are added up.
- In the training data, reviews that contain "thank" get a push of `r f2(mean(S[nhs_matrix[, words == "thank"] > 0, "thank"]))` from it on average.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[The same words on top]{.ct}
*`r paste(vi_tab$Variable[1:5], collapse = ", ")`*: Part II's words.
:::

::: {.fragment}

[SHAP adds direction]{.ct}
*thank*, *helpful*: dots far **left**, towards positive. *get*, *told*: **right**.
:::

::: {.fragment}

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes.

- Left: the bar chart from task 1. `vi()` measures how much the splits on a word improved the trees, added up over all 2,000. It says how much a word is used by the model, not which way it points.
- Middle: the notebook's SHAP plot, top 12 words. Bars: the average absolute push. Dots: one per training review; a dot's position is the push, its colour how much of the word the review has.
- The two rankings agree on the leading words. They are also the words from the keyness plot: a model with 2,000 trees has mostly rediscovered what a count could show, which is reassuring.
- Click: the direction. Reviews that contain "thank" (bright dots) sit far to the left: towards positive. Reviews that contain "told" or "get" sit to the right. Reviews without the word (dark dots) sit close to zero: absence is weak evidence.
- Click: the discussion at line 337. Words that make sense: thank, helpful, friendly, told, phone. Words that surprise: small words such as "one", "just", "still", "never". They are not about anything, but they are how people narrate a bad experience: "still waiting", "just told", "no one". Whether to keep them is a cleaning choice.
:::

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false

(autoplot(cm, type = "heatmap") + theme(text = element_text(size = 14), legend.position = "none")) + f1_plot() + plot_layout(widths = c(1.15, 1))
```

::: {.source-note}
`f_meas()` scores the **first** level, "Negative": how well does the model find the complaints? For "Positive" the test F1 is `r f2(f1_pos)`.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[`r n_wrong` of `r nrow(nhs_test)` test reviews wrong]{.ct}
`r cm$table[2, 1]` complaints called positive, `r cm$table[1, 2]` positive reviews called negative. From 100 words and no word order.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[`r f2(f1_of("Training"))` in training, `r f2(f1_of("Testing"))` in testing]{.ct}
The gap is **overfitting**: 2,000 trees have partly memorised the training reviews. The test score is the honest one.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Another model?]{.ct}
A lasso logistic regression (Lab 3 and 4) on the same recipe: F1 `r f2(f1_lasso)`. Nearly as good, and its coefficients can be read.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 4 minutes.

- The confusion matrix (Lab 4): rows are what the model said, columns the truth. The diagonal is correct: `r cm$table[1, 1]` complaints found, `r cm$table[2, 2]` positive reviews recognised.
- F1 (Labs 4 and 5) combines precision and recall for one class. Which class? tidymodels takes the first factor level, and that is "Negative". So `r f2(f1_of("Testing"))` is about finding complaints, which is probably what a practice would want the model for.
- Click: the training score is far higher than the test score. The model has not seen the test reviews; it has seen the training reviews 2,000 times. Lab 5's point again: never report the training score. Tuning `trees`, `learn_rate` and tree depth with cross-validation would be the next step.
- Click: the discussion at line 384. Good, not perfect: about one review in seven is wrong. Read a few of the errors: many are three-star reviews labelled positive that describe a problem, or sarcasm, or "not helpful" with the "not" removed.
- Other models: lasso logistic regression is the natural rival for text: many columns, most of them irrelevant, and it gives a signed coefficient per word. It scores `r f2(f1_lasso)` here with a penalty that was not tuned. A random forest or naive Bayes are other common answers.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="checks" style="grid-template-columns:1fr">
  <div><b>1</b><span><strong>Text becomes a table</strong> in four steps: corpus, tokens, cleaning, counts. One row per document, one column per word: a <strong>document-feature matrix</strong>. Word order is lost, and every cleaning step is a choice. In code: <code>corpus()</code>, <code>tokens()</code>, <code>tokens_remove(stopwords("en"))</code>, <code>dfm()</code>, <code>dfm_trim()</code></span></div>
  <div><b>2</b><span><strong>Keyness</strong> compares where a word is used with an even split: which words are typical of one group? <strong>TF-IDF</strong> weights a count down when the word is in most documents. In code: <code>textstat_keyness()</code>, <code>step_tfidf()</code></span></div>
  <div><b>3</b><span><strong>The model is Lab 5's</strong>: split, recipe, boosted trees, F1 on the test set. Text steps go <strong>inside the recipe</strong>. <strong>SHAP</strong> explains it one review at a time: a start, a push per word with a direction, and they add up to the prediction</span></div>
</div>
```

**Question:** a new review says "Not helpful at all." What does the model see, and what will it probably predict? What would you change?

::: {.notes}
Wrap-up, 3 minutes.

- Recap in three sentences.
- Exit question: "not", "at" and "all" are stopwords, so the model sees one word, "helpful", which pushes strongly towards positive. It will probably call a complaint positive. Fixes, in order of effort: take "not" and "no" off the stopword list; add bigrams as features, so that "not helpful" is its own column (`step_ngram()`); or use a model that reads words in order, which is where next week goes.
- What to take from today: the modelling was the easy part and nothing in it was new. The decisions that shaped the result were all in turning text into columns.
:::

## Further reading {.closing}

- The completed notebook goes up after class.
- [quanteda tutorials](https://tutorials.quanteda.io): corpus, tokens and DFM step by step, with the same functions as today.
- [*Supervised Machine Learning for Text Analysis in R*](https://smltar.com) (Hvitfeldt and Silge): chapters 2–3 on tokens and stopwords, chapter 7 on classification with `textrecipes`. Free online.
- [*Text Mining with R*](https://www.tidytextmining.com) (Silge and Robinson): chapter 3 on TF-IDF, chapter 4 on bigram networks. Free online.
- [*Interpretable Machine Learning*](https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/) (Molnar): the chapters on Shapley values and SHAP.

::: {.notes}
- Stemming and lemmatisation (treating "appointment" and "appointments" as one word) are mentioned in the notebook's teaching moment and not used. Mention them only if asked: `tokens_wordstem()` in quanteda, `step_stem()` in a recipe.
:::
